case-sara.text: [Softly] Before bed I keep checking his social media even though it wrecks me.
case-sara.suggestion: That pull toward his page fits with how fresh the loss is; each trace offers contact and hurts at the same time.

case-sara.text: [Embarrassed] I smiled through the whole team meeting and then cried in the bathroom afterward.
case-sara.suggestion: Anyone would need room for tears after holding themselves together through that meeting; the tears deserve room rather than embarrassment.

case-sara.text: [Tearful] When I think about the last weeks, I keep wondering if he'd have stayed if I had been more fun or easier.
case-sara.suggestion: Self-blame can look like control when an ending feels helpless; it gives the pain a target even though it turns against you.

case-sara.text: [Softly] At night it gets too quiet, and I start feeling like I was never really wanted.
case-sara.suggestion: In that nighttime quiet, the old not-wanted feeling has room to get loud; loneliness can sound very convincing there.

case-sara.text: [Angry, then embarrassed] A friend told me to stop checking my phone, and I snapped at her.
case-sara.suggestion: No wonder it hit a raw spot; she was treating the phone like a habit, while for you it was still carrying hope.

case-sara.text: [Tearful] When I wake up, I forget for a second and then it slams me.
case-sara.suggestion: Understandably, waking into the loss again is a harsh start to the day; there is no time to protect yourself before it lands.

case-sara.text: [Tearful] I apologize when I start crying, like my sadness is taking up too much room.
case-sara.suggestion: If you have learned to monitor how much space your sadness takes, apologizing for tears makes protective sense; the sadness still belongs here.

case-sara.text: [Embarrassed] I feel guilty for being this upset when I am only dealing with a breakup and other people have bigger problems.
case-sara.suggestion: Comparing losses can make grief feel illegitimate, but being left is still a real wound.

case-sara.text: [Fearful] My friends say I should come out for dinner, but I am scared I will cry at the table.
case-sara.suggestion: Dinner would put a private sadness in public view; fear of crying there is a reasonable wish to protect something tender.

case-sara.text: [Softly] After this breakup, part of me thinks love must be for other people, not me.
case-sara.suggestion: After being left, love can start to look like something reserved for other people; that thought grows out of a very lonely hurt.

case-michael.text: [Guilty] I hit a cyclist with my car last week. The road was slick, but he still broke his wrist and I cannot stop feeling guilty.
case-michael.suggestion: That guilt belongs to the seriousness of what happened: even without intent, your conscience is registering that someone got hurt.

case-michael.text: [Defensive] In meetings, if I don't have the answer, I feel exposed and I bluff.
case-michael.suggestion: When not knowing has been treated like failure, bluffing becomes a shield against humiliation.

case-michael.text: [Tense] When I apologize, it feels like kneeling in front of someone who will use it against me.
case-michael.suggestion: If apology has felt like surrender, your body would brace before offering it; repair can feel unsafe when someone might use it to win.

case-michael.text: [Firm] At home, when my wife sighs or rolls her eyes, I go off before I think.
case-michael.suggestion: A sigh or eye roll can hit the old humiliation channel fast; no wonder your system is defending dignity before you can think.

case-michael.text: [Furious] Watching the news, I get so angry at people in charge acting like consequences are optional.
case-michael.suggestion: That anger has a clear moral charge: when powerful people avoid consequences, it hits your intolerance for unfairness and irresponsibility.

case-michael.text: [Ashamed] When my kid asks why I am angry, I feel like the worst father.
case-michael.suggestion: The shame shows how much safe fatherhood matters to you; his question touches the gap between the dad you want to be and what anger does.

case-michael.text: [Firm] Slamming a door feels awful later, but in the moment it keeps me from feeling small.
case-michael.suggestion: In the moment, the door makes protective sense against feeling small; later the relief turns into pain because it is not how you want to protect yourself.

case-michael.text: [Defensive] If someone challenges me in front of the team, I double down even if I'm wrong.
case-michael.suggestion: Being challenged in public can feel like public demotion; doubling down protects dignity before there is room to be wrong.

case-michael.text: [Ashamed] I hate that I need help with anger; it makes me feel weak.
case-michael.suggestion: If help has meant weakness in your world, even asking for it can feel like standing exposed; the shame is tied to that old rule.

case-michael.text: [Ashamed] After I blow up at home, I lie awake replaying their faces and hating myself.
case-michael.suggestion: No wonder the replay has force; those faces matter to you, and shame is pressing on the part of you that wants them to feel safe.

case-jason.text: [Trembling] Every presentation at work makes my hands shake, and then I feel pathetic for caring so much.
case-jason.suggestion: Under other people's eyes, shaking is an anxious system trying to get through exposure; it is not proof that caring is pathetic.

case-jason.text: [Hesitant] I keep my eyes on the floor so no one has a reason to look at me.
case-jason.suggestion: Keeping your eyes down has protected you from being singled out; visibility has felt risky before it has felt connecting.

case-jason.text: [Anxious] At team lunches, I pretend to text so I have somewhere to hide during small talk.
case-jason.suggestion: The phone gives you a small refuge in small talk; hiding there is a way to survive possible judgment, not a character flaw.

case-jason.text: [Quietly] When people laugh politely after I say something, I assume they are trying to escape me.
case-jason.suggestion: Polite laughter is ambiguous enough for shame to fill in the worst meaning; your mind is trying to protect you from rejection.

case-jason.text: [Hesitant] Compliments bounce off; part of me wants to believe them, but the suspicious part wins.
case-jason.suggestion: When self-attack has had years of practice, praise can feel suspicious before it feels nourishing; the suspicious part is trying to prevent another letdown.

case-jason.text: [Quiet and ashamed] After I talk in a group, I replay every sentence and feel ashamed for sounding awkward.
case-jason.suggestion: The replay is a harsh attempt to keep you from future embarrassment; it makes sense in a world where belonging has felt fragile.

case-jason.text: [Quiet and ashamed] I skipped another team lunch and then felt pathetic for hiding in my apartment.
case-jason.suggestion: Skipping lunch makes protective sense in the moment, and the shame afterward shows the other truth: you still want to belong.

case-jason.text: [Hesitant] I scan every room for who is doing better than me, then feel defective.
case-jason.suggestion: Scanning the room makes anxious sense as your mind tries to find danger and your place; shame turns that scan into a verdict against you.

case-jason.text: [Nervous, almost smiling] Someone invited me to a game night, and I wanted to go for about ten seconds before panic took over.
case-jason.suggestion: No wonder panic rushed in; that same invitation touched both the ten-second hope for connection and the fear of exposure.

case-jason.text: [Quietly] Some nights I lie there certain I will always be alone because I am too awkward to love.
case-jason.suggestion: No wonder nights get heavy; shame can make loneliness sound permanent when the fear has that much room.

case-laura.text: [Flat and ashamed] On days off I can stay in bed until noon, not exactly sleeping, just not able to start. Then I tell myself I am lazy because other people manage normal mornings.
case-laura.suggestion: After years on alert, staying in bed can become the one place with no demands; that belongs to exhaustion and protection, not laziness.

case-laura.text: [Fearful] If voices rise, my stomach drops and I go somewhere else in my head.
case-laura.suggestion: Raised voices can feel like danger fast enough to send you away in your head; that leaving once helped you survive.

case-laura.text: [Guarded and confused] A man from work asked if I wanted coffee, and I felt a tiny bit pleased before I went completely numb. I keep telling myself that is ridiculous at my age.
case-laura.suggestion: Both reactions fit with what closeness has meant: the small warmth of being wanted and the numb protection that arrives when it starts to feel possible.

case-laura.text: [Flat and guarded] I take long showers because warm water feels safer than asking anyone for comfort.
case-laura.suggestion: Small, safe warmth can feel deeply important when human comfort has been dangerous or unreliable.

case-laura.text: [Sad] I like the new apartment, but when I unpacked the photos from the old house, I missed the version of my family I kept hoping we would become.
case-laura.suggestion: The grief belongs to what this move carries: not only a new start but the loss of the home and family you kept trying to have.

case-laura.text: [Tense and guarded] Being touched, even kindly, startles me, and then I feel broken for reacting that way.
case-laura.suggestion: Your startle arriving before choice fits with a system that learned to react first; that is not brokenness.

case-laura.text: [Fearful] When sadness pushes through, I get scared I won't come back from it.
case-laura.suggestion: If strong feelings once arrived without comfort, sadness can feel like it might swallow you.

case-laura.text: [Distant] I apologize the second I need comfort, like wanting it is already too much.
case-laura.suggestion: Wanting comfort is legitimate and deeply human, even when closeness has taught you to apologize for needing it.

case-laura.text: [Flat and embarrassed] My daughter sent a song she thought I would like, and I could not make myself listen. I hate that even something kind feels like work.
case-laura.suggestion: Even kindness can understandably feel demanding after so much guarding; the effort says how hard closeness has become, not that you do not care.

case-laura.text: [Flat and guarded] Even in bed, my shoulders stay up like someone might come through the door.
case-laura.suggestion: Rest can feel hard to find when part of you learned to keep watch for danger.

case-carlos.text: [Tense and angry] Watching the news about families like mine being treated like threats makes me so angry I can barely sit still.
case-carlos.suggestion: That anger fits with dignity, family, and the old fear of being treated as less than fully human.

case-carlos.text: [Tense] If I do not come in strong, I picture people seeing the scared kid I used to be, and that feels humiliating before anyone has even done anything.
case-carlos.suggestion: Coming in strong has protected the scared part you were taught to hide; it also sounds exhausting to keep that armor up.

case-carlos.text: [Ashamed] At my kid's game I yelled at the ref, and afterward my son would not look at me. I keep telling myself I am turning into exactly what I hated.
case-carlos.suggestion: The shame is there because his face matters to you; the yelling needs accountability, and the pain afterward shows how deeply you want to be different.

case-carlos.text: [Defensive] When someone questions me, I feel small, then I come in louder than I meant to.
case-carlos.suggestion: Anger rushing in fits with how quickly questions touch the old feeling of being made small.

case-carlos.text: [Angry and ashamed] When my fists clench, I feel like the fight is already coming, and then I hate myself for looking like every man I promised I would never become.
case-carlos.suggestion: The way your fists clench fits with old survival learning and present shame at the same time; fight was something your body learned to keep you alive.

case-carlos.text: [Ashamed] I break things and then regret it when I see how scared everyone looks.
case-carlos.suggestion: The regret shows how much protecting your family is part of who you want to be.

case-carlos.text: [Ashamed] Coworkers steer clear after I blow up, and I feel ashamed even while I act like I do not care.
case-carlos.suggestion: Shame and armor can feel tangled together: part of you is hurt by the distance, while another part tries not to show it.

case-carlos.text: [Torn] I leave the room so I do not explode, but then I hear my father's voice calling that weak.
case-carlos.suggestion: Leaving fits with protecting your family from the explosion, while also colliding with the old rule that stepping back is weakness.

case-carlos.text: [Mistrustful] Calm feels suspicious, like someone is setting me up to be walked over.
case-carlos.suggestion: Calm can feel exposed after you learned to expect being walked over; suspicion has had a job for a long time.

case-carlos.text: [Vulnerable] My son fell asleep against me on the couch, and I felt proud, scared, and sad all at once because I want him to feel safe with me in a way I never felt.
case-carlos.suggestion: This mix of pride, fear, and sadness belongs to the same moment here; his trust touches your love for him and the grief of not having that kind of safety yourself.

case-nina.text: [Tired] If I sit down before everything is done, guilt starts listing what I should be doing.
case-nina.suggestion: That guilt belongs to the old rule that your worth had to be earned through usefulness.

case-nina.text: [Apologetic] The church asked me to bring food for another event, and I said I could not. I spent the whole night feeling like I had failed at being generous.
case-nina.suggestion: One no can feel morally heavy when generosity and being good have been tied together for so long.

case-nina.text: [Sad and guilty] My husband made dinner without asking me, and instead of just feeling cared for I cried and then apologized for making it strange.
case-nina.suggestion: Being cared for can feel like it touches a deep hunger and a deep alarm at the same time after carrying care alone for so long.

case-nina.text: [Guilty] When anger comes up, I instantly hear myself being selfish and feel guilty.
case-nina.suggestion: Guilt can feel ready to arrive right after anger when you learned that other people's needs had to come first.

case-nina.text: [Apologetic] When I ask for help, I feel like a burden before anyone even answers.
case-nina.suggestion: Needing help can feel risky after years of being the one who carries everyone else.

case-nina.text: [Guilty] A messy counter can make me feel like I have failed as a whole person.
case-nina.suggestion: When care and performance got fused, even mess can feel like shame about who you are.

case-nina.text: [Tired] I tell myself other mothers have it harder, so I should be grateful instead of resentful.
case-nina.suggestion: That comparison can look like an old silencer for your own pain, while resentment can still be a valid signal that you are carrying too much.

case-nina.text: [Apologetic] I work through being sick, then collapse and feel guilty for collapsing.
case-nina.suggestion: Pushing through fits with the rule that rest is forbidden; even the collapse gets judged by that rule.

case-nina.text: [Panicked] If someone seems disappointed, I panic like I have ruined the relationship.
case-nina.suggestion: Disappointment can feel frightening when love has felt tied to keeping people pleased.

case-nina.text: [Torn] My son talks about joining the army, and I feel proud of him and terrified, then guilty because a good mother should be braver.
case-nina.suggestion: This mix of pride and terror belongs to the same moment; loving his courage does not cancel the fear of what his courage may cost him.

case-aisha.text: [Panicked] I watched the door most of session to make sure you won't leave. Every time the hallway got quiet, I thought this might be the moment you decide I am too much and walk out.
case-aisha.suggestion: Keeping the door in view fits with so many sudden endings; it protects against being dropped again, and the need for safety is very real.

case-aisha.text: [Torn] I ripped up photos after the breakup and felt powerful for maybe one minute, like I could erase him first. Then the floor was covered in pieces and I felt empty and ashamed.
case-aisha.suggestion: The tearing gave you a moment of control inside unbearable hurt, and the emptiness afterward belongs to the same loss, not a contradiction.

case-aisha.text: [Panicked] Sometimes the panic gets so loud I want to crawl out of my skin. I pace, scratch at my sleeves, and cannot find a place inside myself that feels safe to stay in.
case-aisha.suggestion: The urge to escape your own skin fits with panic taking over the whole inside; it is an attempt to survive the intensity.

case-aisha.text: [Panicked] When you take notes, I think you are writing proof that I am unstable or too dramatic. I know that may not be fair, but my body wants to bolt before you finish the sentence.
case-aisha.suggestion: Notes can feel like being judged, captured, or misunderstood when other people's versions of you have so often felt dangerous.

case-aisha.text: [Desperate] I send twenty texts because I need them close, then block them before they can leave. Afterward I hate how needy it looks, but in the moment silence feels like being erased.
case-aisha.suggestion: The texting fits with reaching for contact when silence feels unbearable, and blocking tries to protect you from waiting to be abandoned.

case-aisha.text: [Fearful and ashamed] I know it was done to me, but I still feel dirty in my own skin. Sometimes I shower and still feel like there is something wrong with me for having been there.
case-aisha.suggestion: Feeling contaminated after violation can be a painful trauma mark; the shame belongs to what was done to you, not to your worth or your body.

case-aisha.text: [Panicked] When someone says something kind, I sob like I need it and panic like it is a trap. Kindness should feel good, but it makes me feel exposed and hungry at the same time.
case-aisha.suggestion: Kindness can feel like it reaches both the longing for care and the fear of being trapped by needing it after closeness has been so unsafe.

case-aisha.text: [Furious] If you look away for a second, I feel erased and then furious. I know it is one second, but inside it feels like I vanished from the room and have to fight my way back.
case-aisha.suggestion: A tiny shift can feel like proof of disappearing from someone's mind, and the anger tries to restore contact and mattering fast.

case-aisha.text: [Ashamed] I hear a voice saying I am trash and impossible to love, and part of me believes it. It gets loudest after I have needed someone, like need itself proves the voice is right.
case-aisha.suggestion: That cruel voice can sound convincing after betrayal has handed it so much material, especially around the human need for closeness.

case-aisha.text: [Desperate] I stare at the clock to make sure you won't end early. The last five minutes make my chest tight because I am already trying to survive you leaving.
case-aisha.suggestion: Watching the clock fits with bracing for another ending before it takes you by surprise; the fear of being left is already in the room.

case-david.text: [Controlled] When my wife brings up feelings, I feel cornered and want to argue the facts. If I stay with the emotional part, it starts sounding like a trial where I have already lost.
case-david.suggestion: Facts can feel like a defensible place to stand when feelings arrive as accusation; that cornered feeling helps explain why argument takes over so quickly.

case-david.text: [Furious] After I scared my wife, I still felt furious at her for pushing me, and then ashamed because I know how that sounds. I hate admitting that part because I know her fear is real.
case-david.suggestion: It is legitimate to name this painful mixed truth: the rage was genuinely there, and the fear you caused genuinely matters too. Validation can hold both without excusing harm.

case-david.text: [Ashamed] I compare myself to other dads and feel like a fraud. They seem relaxed at school events, and I stand there performing competence while wondering when someone will see through it.
case-david.suggestion: Comparison can feel shame-stirring when fatherhood becomes another performance test in the place you most want to feel solid and real.

case-david.text: [Ashamed] When I apologize, it feels like handing someone proof that I am small. I can know I owe the apology and still feel my face burn like I have given away my last piece of ground.
case-david.suggestion: Apology can feel exposing when it asks for accountability while touching old humiliation about being made small.

case-david.text: [Dismissive] I plan perfect vacations so we look good from the outside. If the photos look happy enough, maybe no one sees how tense dinner was or how little I know what to do at home.
case-david.suggestion: The polished outside has protected against exposure, and it also leaves you carrying the private tension alone after everyone has admired the picture.

case-david.text: [Fearful] The idea of being ordinary scares me, like I would disappear if I stopped impressing people. I do not know who I am without someone needing to admire the result.
case-david.suggestion: If admiration has held your sense of worth together, ordinary can feel like vanishing rather than resting.

case-david.text: [Ashamed] I say I am fine while feeling empty, because admitting the emptiness feels humiliating. I can run a meeting and handle pressure, but saying I feel empty makes me feel pathetic.
case-david.suggestion: The emptiness threatens the competent image that has protected you, so covering it defends against humiliation.

case-david.text: [Dismissive] I brag to get respect, then sit alone feeling emptier than before. The room reacts the way I wanted, and somehow that makes it worse when I am by myself.
case-david.suggestion: The bragging can look like a reach for respect, and the emptiness afterward shows how admiration can steady worth for a moment without touching loneliness.

case-david.text: [Wounded but sharp] I still feel like my father is marking me down from somewhere. I can be in my own office, with my own family, and still hear the grade before I know what I did wrong.
case-david.suggestion: Being measured for so long can feel like it leaves an inner scoreboard that keeps grading even in rooms he no longer controls.

case-david.text: [Controlled] When my team outshines me, I feel threatened instead of proud. I know a good leader should celebrate them, but part of me hears their success as my replacement notice.
case-david.suggestion: Their success can feel like it touches the old equation between being best and being safe, so pride has to compete with the fear of becoming replaceable.

case-marcus.text: [Flat] Most days I move through routines like I am not fully there. I make coffee, shower, answer people, and it feels like a version of me is doing it while the rest stays back.
case-marcus.suggestion: After too much danger, numbness has protected your ability to keep functioning; it is a survival pattern, not a failure to care.

case-marcus.text: [Dazed] I do not know what I feel. It is pressure, anger, and nothing at the same time, and I feel stupid for not having words.
case-marcus.suggestion: Words can disappear when pressure, anger, and numbness arrive together; not knowing belongs to the overwhelm, not to stupidity.

case-marcus.text: [Quiet and guarded] I sit in the car before going inside because I can't face the quiet. The engine is off, but at least the car still feels like a place between the day and the apartment.
case-marcus.suggestion: The car can feel like a buffer before the quiet brings everything back; pausing there doses what feels too much.

case-marcus.text: [Tense] Loud bangs make me jump and then I get angry at myself for reacting. Yesterday a truck gate slammed outside and I was already scanning the room before I knew what happened.
case-marcus.suggestion: Your system moving into survival before choice arrives fits with danger learning; the anger afterward shows how costly it is to live with that reflex.

case-marcus.text: [Low voice] Holidays feel hollow; I don't feel anything I'm supposed to feel. People talk about family and gratitude, and I mostly feel like I am watching through a window.
case-marcus.suggestion: Holidays can feel hollow when they ask for warmth and belonging in the very places where numbness and distance have protected you.

case-marcus.text: [Quiet and guarded] I avoid reminders of my service because they open the floodgates. A news clip or a sound in the street can put me back there faster than I can explain.
case-marcus.suggestion: Avoiding reminders has protected you from being pulled back too fast; the speed of those reactions deserves respect.

case-marcus.text: [Flat] I keep the apartment dark because bright rooms feel like they ask too much of me. With the shades down, I do not have to see the dishes, the empty chair, or myself as clearly.
case-marcus.suggestion: The dim room can feel like a way to lower the demand of being fully present with everything at once; it helps manage exposure.

case-marcus.text: [Low voice] I cannot remember the last time I laughed and trusted it would last. Even when something is funny, I catch myself waiting for the feeling to disappear.
case-marcus.suggestion: Joy can feel hard to trust when your system has had to stay prepared for loss; waiting for it to disappear is part of that protection.

case-marcus.text: [Quiet and guarded] I do not want to need anyone, because needing people has usually meant losing control. If someone matters, they can ask questions, leave, or get inside places I would rather keep closed.
case-marcus.suggestion: Not needing anyone has protected places that have been hurt or invaded; the loneliness is the cost of that protection.

case-marcus.text: [Flat] Sometimes I think I am better off alone forever, because closeness only gives people more ways to hurt me. Alone is not good, exactly, but at least nobody can reach what is left.
case-marcus.suggestion: Aloneness can feel like the only reliable shield after closeness has carried danger, even while it cuts you off from what you also need.
